name.text: Spot the error in a first-principles derivation (INNODEMS)

questiontext.text:
A student differentiates \( f(x) = {@fexpr@} \) from first principles. Their working contains exactly one mistake. Read each line carefully.

Line 1:  \( f(x+h) = {@D1@} \)

Line 2:  \( f(x+h) - f(x) = {@D2@} \)

Line 3:  \( \displaystyle\dfrac{f(x+h) - f(x)}{h} = {@D3@} \)

Line 4:  \( \displaystyle f'(x) = \lim_{h \to 0}\dfrac{f(x+h) - f(x)}{h} = {@D4@} \)

Which line contains the first mistake?

[[input:wl]] [[validation:wl]] [[feedback:prtwl]]

Now write the corrected right-hand side of that line:

\( \phantom{x} = \) [[input:fix]] [[validation:fix]] [[feedback:prtfix]]

generalfeedback.text:
The first mistake is on Line {@first_wrong@}: {@err_name@}

The correct working from first principles is:

\[ \begin{align*} f(x+h) &= {@C1@} \\[2pt] f(x+h) - f(x) &= {@C2@} \\[2pt] \frac{f(x+h) - f(x)}{h} &= {@C3@} \\[2pt] f'(x) = \lim_{h \to 0}\left({@C3@}\right) &= {@C4@}. \end{align*} \]

A good habit: re-derive each line yourself and compare. The first line that disagrees with your own working is where the error is - even if a later line (or the final answer) happens to look correct.

questionnote.text: \( f(x)={@fexpr@} \); errtype {@errtype@}; first wrong = Line {@first_wrong@}; fix \( = {@correct_fix@} \)

node.description: Corrected line matches the correct RHS?

truefeedback.text: That is the line exactly as the student wrote it - you need to correct the mistake, not copy it. Work out what that right-hand side should be.

falsefeedback.text: That is not the correct right-hand side for this line. Re-derive it carefully from the previous (correct) line.

feedbackvariables.text: /* Did the student blame a line that is actually still correct (too early)? */ too_early : is(wl < first_wrong);

truefeedback.text: Not quite - the line you chose is actually correct. Check it against your own working, then look further down for the first line that goes wrong.

falsefeedback.text: Look again - there is an earlier line that already contains a mistake. Re-derive each line yourself, starting from Line 1, and stop at the first one that disagrees.
